composition: Nominal composition Fe–20Mn–9Al-1.5C–2Ni–3Cr (wt.%), with the analyzed ingot composition Fe-20.3Mn-8.6Al-1.4C-2.1Ni-2.9Cr (wt.%), produced by vacuum induction melting. Iron is the balance. Al is added to lower the density — the measured density is 6.78 g/cm³, about 14 % below that of pure iron (7.87 g/cm³), consistent with the ~1.5 % density reduction per 1 wt% Al; it also drives κ-carbide precipitation. Mn stabilizes austenite, C provides interstitial solid solution and κ-carbide formation, Ni promotes the B2 phase with Al, and Cr is added for corrosion resistance and to inhibit κ-carbide formation. The austenite chemistry measured by EDS for the S1000 condition is Mn 20.97 ± 0.34, Al 9.30 ± 0.02, Ni 2.04 ± 0.26, Cr 3.24 ± 0.78 and C 1.17 ± 0.13 (wt.%, C calculated from the lattice parameter), Fe balance — essentially identical to the S1050 and MHT austenite, so compositional differences do not account for the property differences between conditions.
summary: S1000 is the single-stage-heat-treated condition of the Fe–20Mn–9Al-1.5C–2Ni–3Cr low-density (lightweight) austenitic steel studied by Xiao et al. It was obtained by holding the hot-rolled sheet at 1000 °C for 3 min and water-quenching to room temperature, producing a fully austenitic matrix with annealing twins, nanoscale κ-carbides, and elongated stripe-like Cr7C3 precipitates along the grain boundaries. In the paper's comparison of single-stage (S1000, S1050) and multi-stage (MHT) heat treatments, S1000 defines the high-strength/low-toughness end-member: it retains the highest yield and tensile strength (955 ± 7 MPa, 1126 ± 3 MPa) and elongation (55.5 ± 1.3 %) but the lowest room-temperature Charpy impact energy (29.2 ± 2.0 J), and is used to establish how intergranular Cr7C3 precipitates degrade crack-propagation resistance.
